notes.title: v2.00 Now Available
notes.content:
v2.00 of [i]Dissent on Mars[/i] is now live! There’s a brand new tutorial that’s broken up into eight chapters. We think it does a better job showing how the different economies work and will help with the steep learning curve. It’s broken up into digestible chunks, and there are challenges along the way to test your knowledge. Just like the old tutorial, you can enable it while designing a new society.

We hope this helps, and that you’ll help spread the word by leaving a review and telling your friends! Here’s the full list of updates:

[h1]Tutorial[/h1]
- Added a new tutorial.
- Changed the tutorial textbox to move with the arrow.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
- Changed the plan creator logic in democratic planning so everyone can become the plan creator, not just the people who work there.
- Added an option to select colonists from a workplace’s Members menu.
- Changed the stat boxes that appear to the right in some menus to update while you’re changing values.

[h1]Options[/h1]
- Added a master volume.

[h1]Bug Fixes[/h1]
- Fixed a bug where generating a forest could freeze the game.

[h1]Other[/h1]
- Changed the text to be clearer in a few places.

Hope you enjoy,

Michael

Michael

notes.title: Devlog #4
notes.content:
Hey everyone,

Just wanted to give a quick update about what I’ve been doing. I’ve decided to recreate the tutorial from the ground up. The new tutorial will be broken up into multiple chapters and have challenges along the way to test your knowledge. There will also be a larger focus on showing how the different economic systems work since this is the brain that drives the whole game.

I’m making good progress, but there’s still a lot to do. I’ll keep you updated as it moves along!

Thanks for reading,

Michael

notes.title: Future Plans
notes.content:
Thanks to everyone who has been playing [i]Dissent on Mars[/i]! We really appreciate the support. Now that some time has passed, I’d like to talk about my plans for the future.

There are two things I’d like to address: 1. the wrong impressions people are getting before playing, and 2. the steep learning curve.

The art style for [i]Dissent on Mars[/i] is similar to [i]Prison Architect[/i] and [i]Rimworld[/i]. Unfortunately, I think this has been giving some folks the impression that it’s a clone. To be clear: this is a game about designing different economies and governments, living in them, and seeing their impact on people. In response, I’ve removed the Colony Sim tag from our page. Hopefully, this will help clear things up.

The most important thing I’d like to work on now is making the game easier to get into. It has a steep learning curve, so I’m thinking about ways to make things more digestible. I’m the only programmer, and we don’t have any kind of outside support, so I hope you’ll be patient with me as I figure out the best path forward.

Thanks again,

Michael

notes.title: Soundtracks Now Available
notes.content:
I’m excited to announce that the soundtracks I made for [i]Dissent on Mars[/i] are now available! There’s the [i]Dissent on Mars: Daytime Soundtrack[/i] and the [i]Dissent on Mars: Nighttime Soundtrack[/i]. You can buy them on Steam ([url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/2141450/Dissent_on_Mars_Daytime_Soundtrack/]here[/url] and [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/2141480/Dissent_on_Mars_Nighttime_Soundtrack/]here[/url]), or Bandcamp ([url=https://michaelarts.bandcamp.com/album/dissent-on-mars-daytime-soundtrack]here[/url] and [url=https://michaelarts.bandcamp.com/album/dissent-on-mars-nighttime-soundtrack]here[/url]). If you’d like to wait for a small discount, they’ll be included in a Deluxe Edition of the game that will launch on Monday.

If you like spacey ambient music, I think these will be right up your alley! The first song on both albums was written in my college apartment back in 2011. I wanted to make a soundtrack that mixed other-worldly synthesizers with natural-sounding instruments. I wrote that song and several others for a game I ended up abandoning.

Fast forward 11 years, and I felt my vision for the old soundtrack fit perfectly with [i]Dissent on Mars[/i]. I used the first song as a starting point and made the remaining 11 songs over a few months in 2022. Most of the songs took 3 days to make. The first day was for improvising a synthesizer part, the second was for improvising a melody, and the third was for a quick mix and mastering job. Sometimes it took a little longer. The whole thing felt like a jazz session; I would play some random notes and see where it took me.

This is the simplest batch of songs I’ve ever made; there are never more than two instruments on a track. My last few soundtracks are very dense, so it felt good to do something more stripped back. I hope you enjoy them!

Thanks for listening,

Michael

notes.title: Coming to Steam on April 7th
notes.content:
Finally, after 5+ years of development, [i]Dissent on Mars[/i] is coming to Steam on April 7th! To help celebrate, we’ve released an updated version of the trailer. Check it out:

[previewyoutube=B3lOE20gH-k;full][/previewyoutube]
Nothing is perfect, but I can honestly say I’ve put everything I have into this game. This has been a dream project of mine for 13 years, and it’s hard to put into words how it feels to finally be here. This wouldn’t be happening without the help of many people, so I’d like to take the time to thank some of them.

First, thanks to Gonçalo Antunes for drawing the art. I’ve collaborated with him on every game I’ve made since 2012, and it’s hard to imagine doing this with anyone else. Besides drawing, he brings his own creative ideas to the table, and makes the development process a lot more fun! It always helps to have a friend around.

Thanks to my parents Chuck and Dee. I quit my job in High School to make indie games and then moved in with them after college to try doing it full-time. Thanks to them we were able to ship our first big project back in 2015. I don’t think it’s possible to have more supportive parents, and I’m beyond grateful for their love, support, and inspiration. I dedicate this game to the memory of my dad, rest in peace.
 
Thanks to my friends and family for being there for me, and for testing the game! This would turn into a book if I wrote a paragraph for everyone, but I want to specifically thank Adrian Garcia who has been one of my best friends for over 20 years. He’s usually one of the first people to test a new game, and hearing his thoughts is always something I look forward to.

Thanks to everyone who’s thinking about different ways of running an economy and government. I wanted this game to let people experiment with a variety of different setups, so I spent a lot of time researching different proposals. I specifically want to thank Robin Hahnel, Jason Chrysostomou, Michael Weisdorf, and Mitchell Szczepanczyk for going above and beyond in answering my questions and letting me conduct lengthy interviews. I also had the chance to interview Jacque Fresco in person. Listening to his talks pushed me towards making this game, so I’m glad I was able to meet him before he passed away. Hopefully, I can live to be 101 too!

Thanks to Jason Rohrer, who has been my game design hero for many years. Playing [i]Gravitation[/i] helped me realize that video games can have a deeper impact on people. Jason sent some important emails throughout the years that helped me grow and not give up. The feedback he sent for the [i]Dissent on Mars[/i] trailer was invaluable and the trailer is much better because of it.

Thanks to the Xbox Live Indie Games community for helping me realize I could become an indie game developer. Growing up I never thought any of this was possible, but XNA changed everything. I learned so much from that community, and it was great to be around people who were usually making games for the love of doing it and not for the love of money. I made lifelong friends there, and it’s been inspiring to see what so many of them have gone on to accomplish.

And finally, last but not least, thanks to all of the fans! Reading messages from excited fans was the fuel I needed to get to the finish line. I hope you enjoy playing the game! I definitely enjoyed developing it.

We’re almost there!!

Michael

notes.title: Random Events pt. 2
notes.content:
Different types of random events can occur in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i]. In this post, we’re going to talk about random events that may require some detective work to address.

[h1]Detective Events[/h1]
I tried designing a randomly generated detective game many years ago and was never happy with it. I’m glad I was finally able to scratch that itch with some of the events in this game! Here are some you can expect to see:

[b]Missing Colonist[/b] – If a colonist is missing, you’ll need to find them, which is easier said than done. If you can track down their house, you may find clues that give hints to their location.

[b]Sickness[/b] – Sometimes a product defect will cause colonists to get sick. You’ll need to deduce which one is causing their sickness and recall it at a government building.

[b]Theft[/b] – Theft may occur in the colony, and if it does, you’ll need to deduce who the thief is and charge them. You’ll also need to figure out their motive for stealing. For example, the thief could have an economic motive, or they could be a kleptomaniac!

[b]Work Stoppage[/b] – If the colony has a work stoppage, you’ll need to deduce which workplace is experiencing the stoppage and send someone to work there.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of how random events work. There are even more I haven’t covered, so hopefully they’re a nice surprise when you experience them in the game!

notes.title: Random Events pt. 1
notes.content:
Different types of random events can occur in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i]. In this post, we’re going to talk about news stories, which can be used to influence people’s behavior in the colony.

[h1]News Stories[/h1]
If your colony has a news center, colonists can report on stories from around the solar system. Some stories require the reporter to have a specific charisma skill, so you may not be able to report on everything. Most news stories impact the demand for products, but some have other effects. Here are some you can expect to see:

[b]Albums Are Propaganda[/b] - A viewer claims that all albums have Satanic messaging if you listen to them in reverse.

[b]Game Industry Boycotted[/b] - The game industry has been criticized for being uncreative. Gamers are calling for a boycott until developers start experimenting with new designs.

[b]Smartphones Upgraded[/b] - Remember that smartphone you bought yesterday? It’s time to buy another one!

[b]Walkie-Talkie Signals UFO[/b] - A radio enthusiast claims to have signaled a UFO with their walkie-talkie.

[b]Workers Ask for Top Pay[/b] - A labor union is calling for all Martian workers to ask for the highest hourly income possible.

If it’s not obvious, the positive-sounding product stories can increase demand, while the negative-sounding ones can decrease demand. In the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2138560/view/547854206358259129]last post[/url], we talked about short-term goals, and I’m guessing many of you will use news stories as part of your strategy for achieving them.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of how news stories work. In my next post, I’m going to talk about random events that may require some detective work to address.

notes.title: Goals pt. 2
notes.content:
There are different types of goals you can achieve in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i]. In the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2138560/view/574874782030364685]last post[/url], we talked about global goals and long-term goals. Today, we’re going to look at short-term goals, which are randomly generated based on colonist requests.

[h1]Short-Term Goals[/h1]
Many different short-term goals can appear, and the objectives may be different each time you see them. For simplicity’s sake, I’m just going to show you a few of my favorites: 

[b]House Wanted[/b] – Sometimes colonists will want to live in a new house that’s custom-built for them. I usually play the game hyper-focused on the economic goals, so this goal is a nice change of pace for me. I enjoy chilling and building a house that fits someone’s personality.

[b]No Job Wanted[/b] – In a [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2138560/view/530960814475051536]previous post[/url], we talked about traits and how they can influence a colonist’s behavior. If a colonist is lazy, they may want to be the only person who isn’t employed. In some economies, this can be a real challenge, and you’ll need to think systemically to come up with a solution.

[b]Product Buddy Wanted[/b] – Sometimes colonists will want to use a product alongside someone else. For example, they may want to have a meal with someone. It gives me a warm fuzzy feeling to achieve this goal, but it also presents an opportunity to build parks and other public spaces where people can do things together.

[b]Sabotage Wanted[/b] – If a colonist is a rebel, they may want you to sabotage a business! You’ll need to make sure an owner doesn’t receive any income for ownership, and nothing puts a bigger grin on my face than watching a filthy rich colonist not make any money!

[b]Top Product Wanted[/b] – A lot of the goals in this game revolve around the economy, and this one is a perfect example of that. Colonists may want a certain product to be one of the top-selling products in the colony. There’s a menu where you can see the ranking of each product, and you’ll need to figure out different ways to influence the economy to achieve this goal!

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of how short-term goals work in the game. In combination with global goals and long-term goals, I think you’ll have plenty of things to do!

notes.title: Goals pt. 1
notes.content:
There are different types of goals you can achieve in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i]. In this post, we’re going to look at global goals and long-term goals, which are used together to compare the performance of different societies.

[h1]Long-Term Goals[/h1]
Long-term goals measure the performance of your society using a variety of different metrics. Here are some you can expect to see:

[b]An Efficient Economy[/b] - Create an economy that meets everyone’s needs while achieving minimum waste.

[b]Low Economic Inequality[/b] - Create a society where income and wealth inequality is low.

[b]Martian Job Lovers I[/b] - Create a society where everyone loves their job.

[b]No Poverty[/b] - Create a society where no one lives in poverty.

[b]No Unemployment[/b] - Create a society where there’s no unemployment.

These goals measure the impacts of your society on everyone, not just your main character. The most important one is called “Living Utopia”, and it requires you to do all of these things and more without the government intervening. Most testers think this one is the hardest!

[h1]Global Goals[/h1]
Global goals can be achieved across every society on Mars, and they’re used to keep track of how many long-term goals you’ve achieved with different societies. Here’s an example:

[b]Long-Term Achiever I[/b] - Achieve 7 long-term goals with every system across all societies.

The ultimate goal of the game is to compare different societies by achieving goals. Each society has different pros and cons, so each goal's difficulty will change based on your design. For example, you may find that it’s harder to achieve low economic inequality in one type of society, but easier in another.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of how global goals and long-term goals work in the game. In my next post, I’m going to talk about short-term goals which are randomly generated based on colonist requests.

notes.title: Laws pt. 2
notes.content:
Each colony in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i] has laws that provide additional rules based on the constitution. In the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2138560/view/501688685554565393]last post[/url], we started exploring some of the laws. Today, I’d like to talk about the last batch of laws your colony can have.

[h1]Consumption Rights[/h1]
The constitution determines the different ways colonists can receive income, but some of the amounts they receive are set by laws. For example, you can set how much income each colonist receives for need. You can also set how much income colonists receive for an hour of work.

[h1]Wealth Redistribution[/h1]
If personal property is owned by the state, you can enact a law that redistributes the colony’s wealth by confiscating personal property. For example, you could authorize the government to redistribute wealth from the rich to the poor, or you could redistribute it in a way that benefits a specific colonist.

[h1]Wealth Tax[/h1]
If money is transferable, you can edit the colony’s wealth tax. This lets you set how much wealth colonists can have before being taxed, and the percentage of a colonist’s excess wealth that can be taxed. If taxes aren’t your thing, you can also disable it!

[h1]Product Recall[/h1]
Sometimes products may have defects that make colonists sick. If this happens, you can enact a law that asks workplaces to recall a product. If defects are found, workplaces will fix the products before returning them.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of how laws work in the game. Now, here’s the real question: what types of laws will be enacted in your society?

notes.title: Laws pt. 1
notes.content:
Each colony in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i] has a constitution that determines the rules for how the colony operates. In previous posts, we’ve explored the different parts of a constitution: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3693569804226260180]allocation systems[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3714963077086795214]property rights[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3895115310535792009]money[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3982937405673735196]consumption rights[/url], and [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/547848028756640316]decision making[/url]. Today, I’d like to talk about laws, which provide additional rules based on the constitution.

[h1]Revolution[/h1]
If enough people are protesting, you can declare a revolution and design a new constitution. Hopefully, you can find solutions to the colonist’s problems without abolishing the whole government, but hey, sometimes you’ve gotta do what you’ve gotta do!

[h1]Product Policy[/h1]
This law determines what types of products colonists can buy at a distribution center. They can either buy any product that’s available, or they can only buy products that were included in their consumption plan. If the colony uses democratic planning, colonists will create consumption plans that signal what they plan to buy. Changing the product policy prevents them from buying things that weren’t included in their plan.

[h1]Surplus Limit[/h1]
If the colony uses democratic planning, a supercomputer called the allocation computer calculates the supply and demand for everything in the economy based on the colonist’s plans. If everything is feasible, the plans will be approved. The surplus limit determines when the allocation computer considers a product feasible. For example, if the surplus limit is 5%, every product in the colony would need to have a surplus of 5% or less to be considered feasible.

[h1]Round Limits[/h1]
If the colony uses democratic planning, colonists will negotiate how the economy works through multiple rounds of planning. Since negotiations can go on forever, there needs to be limits on how long they can last. Two laws help with this: the first sets a limit for how many rounds in a row a product can be unfeasible before it’s forbidden, and the second sets a limit for how many rounds can occur before all products are forbidden. The colonists will try to negotiate a feasible plan, but if there are some products they can’t agree on they’ll eventually be forbidden. If the negotiations continue to go on for a long time, the second limit ensures the process will come to an end.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
I’m guessing this post gave you a lot to chew on, so I’ll talk about the remaining laws in the next post!

notes.title: Traits
notes.content:
Each colonist in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i] has a unique personality that determines how they behave. Today, I’d like to talk about some of the traits colonists can have and how they impact the game!

[h1]Bootlicker[/h1]
In the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/547848028756640316]last article[/url], we talked about the different ways decisions can be made in a workplace. Depending on their personality traits, some colonists may prefer having input, while others may like being told what to do. Can you guess what bootlickers love to do? If it’s not obvious, bootlickers love being told what to do and hate making their own decisions. They’ll gravitate towards jobs where they can be bossed around, and they’ll lick those boots with a huge smile on their face.

[h1]Rebel[/h1]
Rebels are the opposite of bootlickers: they hate being told what to do! Rebels avoid jobs where they have no input, and they may stir up some trouble in the colony. For example, rebels may want you to sabotage a business owned by a wealthy colonist, or they may even start a rebellion and refuse to work!

[h1]Hard Worker[/h1]
When colonists apply for jobs, they’ll need to decide how long they want to work. Several things influence this decision, but a major one is their work ethic. Hard workers have a high work ethic, and they tend to work for as long as they possibly can. Colonists can also be lazy, but I’m sure no one will be like that in your colony, right?

[h1]Greedy[/h1]
Greedy colonists buy more products than needed and charge higher prices for products. One time I was testing the game and took my colonist to the store. I was in the mood for some pepperoni pizza, but my mood quickly changed after realizing it would cost 88 credits, which is pretty high for Martian pizza! I looked into it, and sure enough, a greedy colonist was gouging prices at the pizzeria. Luckily, he went out of business after I built my own pizzeria and undercut his prices! Virtual pepperoni pizza never tasted so good.

[h1]Gameaholic[/h1]
Traits can determine what types of products fulfill a colonist’s needs. As you might expect, the only thing that fulfills a gameaholic’s fun need is video games! Films, books, and albums just don’t cut it for these people. Some traits also determine how many products a colonist needs to consume. For example, introverts don’t need to socialize as much as extroverts, so they don’t need to consume as many social products.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of how the colonist’s traits can impact the game. Now, here’s the real question: what types of colonists will live in your society?

notes.title: Decision Making
notes.content:
Over the last year, we’ve dived into the different choices you have for designing a society in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i]. We’ve talked about [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3693569804226260180]allocation systems[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3714963077086795214]property rights[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3895115310535792009]money[/url], and [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3982937405673735196]consumption rights[/url]. Today, we’re diving into the final choice: decision making.

Depending on how productive property is owned, workplaces may have an individual owner or a group of owners. So, how should owners make decisions inside of a workplace? In [i]Dissent on Mars[/i], your answer to this question changes the rules of the game.

[h1]Autocratic[/h1]
If decisions are made autocratically, one person or group makes decisions and everyone else follows. The decisions could be made by a private owner, a government official, or an elected manager. For example, if someone owns a bakery, the owner will make all of the decisions regarding what to produce, how long everyone works, and so on. No one else has input in these decisions. Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you probably know this is how most workplaces work on Earth.

However, if a workplace has multiple owners, they can elect someone to be the decision maker. The other owners won’t have input in specific decisions (what to produce, how long to work etc.), but they can at least decide who gets to be the autocrat. If there are people in the workplace who aren’t owners, they have no input in who’s elected.

Maybe this is a controversial thing to say, but I think this is how most “democratic” political systems work in the world today. We have input in who’s elected to represent us, but once they’re elected, there are few (if any) ways for us to have input in the specific decisions they make on our behalf. Unless, of course, you have a briefcase full of cash to donate to their campaign!

[h1]Democratic[/h1]
If decisions are made democratically, decisions are made collectively and each owner has input in proportion to how much they’re affected by a decision. If there’s a group of owners, they’ll elect someone to be the decision maker, but they can also have input in specific decisions. For example, if the decision maker creates a work schedule that unfairly benefits them, the owners could vote for them to create a fairer schedule. If the decision maker continues to do things the owners disagree with, they can immediately recall them and elect someone else.

To be clear: this doesn’t mean that every single decision requires a vote. If the owners are happy with the decision maker they can let them be. However, if they plan to do something the majority of owners disagree with, there are mechanisms in place to let them have input.

I wasn’t able to model this in as much detail, but notice I said that owners have “input in proportion to how much they’re affected by a decision.” In the game, all of the workplace decisions impact everyone so each owner has a say. But in the real world, some decisions may impact one group of people while not impacting others at all. For example, if the animators at a game studio need to decide what software to use, it doesn’t make sense for the audio department to have a say since it doesn’t affect them.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of how decisions can be made in a workplace! In short, owners can make decisions autocratically or democratically, and who’s considered an owner depends on how productive property is owned.

Now, here’s the real question: how will workplaces make decisions in your society?

notes.title: Consumption Rights
notes.content:
Having an income lets people buy products, but which principles should determine how we receive income? In Dissent on Mars, your answer to this question changes the rules of the game.

Let’s dive into these concepts so you can see how they work in-game!

[h1]For Need[/h1]
If citizens receive income for need, income could be provided to cover everyone’s need for food, hygiene, and more. Once your colony is built, you can set the exact amount at a government building.

[h1]For Ownership[/h1]
If citizens receive income for ownership, they’ll receive income based on the productive property they own. For example, if someone owns a factory, the owner will receive income based on what the factory sells. 

This principle is dependent on how [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2138560/view/3714963077086795213]productive property[/url] is owned. For example, this can’t work if productive property is owned by the state, or if it’s shared by everyone in society.

[h1]For Power[/h1]
If citizens receive income for power, they’ll receive income based on the amount of bargaining power they have to negotiate prices. 

To enable this principle, your society will need to use a market for [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2138560/view/3693569804226260179]resource allocation[/url].

If you’re unsure what I mean by “bargaining power”, imagine there’s a producer that has a monopoly on food. Since there’s no competition, they could gouge their prices to the sky, therefore receiving more income. If there was more competition, this would be harder to pull off since the competitors could keep their prices low, potentially taking business away from the price gouger.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44505437/46600b3402788dcc4b6fc465acf21579d1f8c5bc.png[/img]

[h1]For Work[/h1]
If citizens receive income for work, they’ll receive income based on the amount of work they put in towards an economic activity.

This principle is pretty self-explanatory, and I imagine most people reading this are already familiar with how it works!

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of the different ways people can receive income! In short, citizens can receive income for need, ownership, power, or work.

Now, here’s the real question: how will citizens receive income in your society?

notes.title: Money
notes.content:
As we get deeper into the holiday season, I think it’s a good time to tackle a subject that’s on everyone’s mind. We love it, we hate it, we chase it… yup, you guessed it: money! Let’s dive into how it works in [i]Dissent on Mars[/i].

The first thing you should know is that Martians don’t use the same currency as Earthlings, so don’t expect to see any dollars, pounds, or euros. Instead, they use a new currency called credits. Here’s what the symbol looks like:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44505437/cf06818035f4f032d8558343be3969fd8568d886.png[/img]

To keep track of their credits, each colonist has an income card. These are used to make purchases and will record how money was spent or received, which may be useful if you want to see how someone amassed their wealth.

[h1]Accumulable and Transferable[/h1]
Just like [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3693569804226260180]allocation systems[/url] and [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/2138560/announcements/detail/3714963077086795214]property rights[/url], you can change the rules for how money works while designing your society. You’ll need to decide if money is accumulable and transferable.

If you decide it shouldn’t be accumulable, everyone’s income card will be cleared after a length of time.

If you decide it shouldn’t be transferable, money will only be usable by the first person who receives it, and it will only be accepted to buy new products.

If your colony uses a market, money must be accumulable and transferable since that’s the only way a market can work.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Now that you know how money works, we need to talk about the different ways people can receive it. This will be my first post in 2024!

I hope everyone has a great holiday season and a happy new year! 2023 had an insane amount of work for me, but seeing people excited to play makes everything worth it. I can’t wait to share more with you next year!

notes.title: Property Rights
notes.content:
Every society has different types of property such as natural resources, buildings, and personal goods, but who should have control over them? In [i]Dissent on Mars[/i], your answer to this question changes the rules of the game.

Property can be categorized as productive property or personal property, and there are different ways it can be owned. 

Let’s dive into these concepts so you can see how they work in-game!

[h1]Ownership[/h1]
There are four different ways property can be owned, and here’s how they’re defined:

[b]Common Ownership[/b]
The property is inherited by all the world’s people and is freely available to everyone. 

[b]Cooperative Ownership[/b]
The property is owned by democratically controlled groups.

[b]Private Ownership[/b]
The property is owned by private individuals.

[b]State Ownership[/b]
The property is owned by a governing body that represents the public.

[h1]Productive Property[/h1]
Productive property includes natural resources (such as land, water, and plants), workplaces that make products for the public, and anything else used in production. 

The [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/2138560/view/3693569804226260179]allocation system[/url] you select determines how productive property can be owned since each system uses productive property in different ways.

For example, in market economies, productive property could be owned by a group of workers (cooperative ownership), or by a single person (private ownership).

In centrally planned economies, productive property is owned by the state since a central authority is creating a plan for the entire economy. 

In democratically planned economies, productive property is owned commonly since producers and consumers are working together to create a plan for the entire economy.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44505437/6ad9c78c9aef8bd94c268140cdf9af1ba023be94.png[/img]
[h1]Personal Property[/h1]
Personal property includes items intended for personal use such as food, furniture, and houses. 

Unlike productive property, personal property can be owned privately or by the state, regardless of the allocation system you select.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Hopefully, this gives you an idea of all the different ways property can be owned in the game! In short, property is categorized by its intended use, and it could be controlled by everyone in society, multiple groups, multiple individuals, or by the state.

Now, here’s the real question: how will property be owned in your society?

notes.title: Allocation Systems
notes.content:
Every society has natural resources and labor that are required to make products, but how do we decide what products to make and which resources to use? In [i]Dissent on Mars[/i], your answer to this question changes the rules of the game.

There are three different allocation systems an economy can use: a market, central planning, and democratic planning. Most people are familiar with markets since that’s the main one we use on Earth, but you can use any of them on Mars!

Let’s dive into each one so you have a better idea of how they work in-game.

[h1]Market[/h1]
A market is a competitive bidding between producers and consumers. Producers bring products to the market and adjust decisions based on consumer demand.

For example, if your colony produced 200 bottles of orange juice but only 10 bottles were sold, producers would likely lower the price to increase their chances of selling it. The lowered price also incentivizes producers to make less orange juice in the future. If demand was greater than supply, the price would likely increase, therefore incentivizing producers to make more of it.

Bargaining power also plays a big role in how markets work. The classic example of this is a monopoly; if one producer controls an entire industry, nothing is stopping them from gouging their prices to the sky. Since you can control any character you want, this monopolist could be you… but we shouldn’t have to worry about that, right? I’m sure Martians would never be greedy!

[h1]Central Planning[/h1]
In central planning, a central authority collects information and creates a plan for the entire economy. The central authority can either be you (the player) or a computer that monitors the economy.

The central planner is responsible for setting the prices of every product, allocating labor into workplaces, creating production plans for workplaces, and more. The fact that these decisions are centralized makes it easy to run the economy in different ways. For example, you could adjust prices based on supply and demand, or you could make everything incredibly cheap to help out the colonists.

Of course, being a central planner comes with a lot of responsibility. The entire colony is depending on you to do a good job, so let’s hope you’re up to the task!


[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/44505437/e95b1dd1c5e953f7977a35ea4b198dd12a5a75a2.png[/img]

[h1]Democratic Planning[/h1]
In democratic planning, producers and consumers work together to create a plan for the entire economy. In some ways, this is the inverse of a market; instead of encouraging competition, this system encourages cooperation.

Throughout this process, producers create plans listing what they’d like to produce, while consumers create plans listing what they’d like to consume. The plans are then analyzed by a computer to determine the supply and demand for everything in the economy. If everything is feasible, the plans will be approved. Otherwise, prices will be updated by a computer, and the colonists will adjust their plans accordingly.

You can think of this as a “virtual negotiation”. Instead of negotiating verbally in person, it’s being done with the colonists’ plans. Of course, we all know that democracy can sometimes be messy and drawn out… so I wonder how long it will take your colonists to negotiate a plan for the entire economy?

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Honestly, this post only gives a brief overview of how these systems work, but I hope it gives you an idea of the different directions you can take your society. 

I’m guessing you have a lot of questions, but don’t worry! There’s more information coming. In my next post, I’m going to talk about property and the different ways it can be owned. I hope you’re looking forward to it!
